note: Dorian against Mixolydian, told apart by the 3rd: heard in a two-scales play-along over a drone, then phrases ending on {{b3}} in Dorian and on {{3}} in Mixolydian in the same frets, with the minor 3rd added as a note outside the scale to slide from. The key is now moves (any key), named only as {{=key}}; every note is a degree token, so it moves with the key, and the last line says what stays the same in another key.

exercise.title: Dorian or Mixolydian: the 3rd
exercise.why: Dorian and Mixolydian on one root share six notes and differ only in the 3rd, so moving that one note a fret turns the minor mode into the major one.

cells.text:
Press Play below to start the backing track: a drone on {{=key}}, with four bars of {{=key}} Dorian and then four bars of {{=key}} Mixolydian. Play each scale along with the neck, from the lowest note up to the highest and back down.
Listen for the bar where the 3rd moves: the faded note is the one to leave out, {{3}} in the Dorian half and {{b3}} in the Mixolydian half.

Below is the neck with the position of {{=key}} Dorian that has {{1}} on the low E string: each dot is a note to play, with {{1}} and {{b3}} ringed.
Start on {{1}} on the low E string, play up to the high e string and back down, then make up a few short phrases that end on {{b3}}.

Below are the same frets in {{=key}} Mixolydian: the 3rd has moved up a fret, to the ringed {{3}}. Play the phrases you made up again and end them on {{3}}.
Then slide into {{3}} from one fret below. That note is {{b3}}, not in Mixolydian: it is the minor 3rd you just left, and sliding from it up to {{3}} is a sound blues players use all the time.
{{?key}}In another key the position sits on other frets, and the 3rd still moves by one fret between the two modes.
